TWO COORDINATE SYSTEMS, and confusing them silently misbuilds the gold: `source_char_span` is where the block sits in the source file and is exported for traceability only, while a citation's char_span indexes into the block's own `text` from 0 — that is what faithfulness_gate._entails slices when it puts a premise to the judge (`block.text[start:end]`). Author pairs against `text` and bound them by `text_length`; never copy `source_char_span` into a pair.

blocks.text: API REST conventions

The darkmem HTTP API (`/api/v1/*`) follows REST for true resources and a small,
consistent set of pragmatic patterns for everything else. This document is the
contract: new endpoints should match it, and the documented deviations should
not regress.
Resource CRUD
True resources use standard verbs and status codes:

| Action | Verb | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Create | `POST /collection` | `201 Created` |
| Read one | `GET /collection/{id}` | `200` |
| Read list | `GET /collection` | `200` |
| Replace / update | `PUT /collection/{id}` (full), `PATCH` (partial) | `200` |
| Delete | `DELETE /collection/{id}` | `204 No Content` (no body) |

Examples: `memories`, `repos`, `chat/conversations`, the config singletons.
Collections are plural nouns; sub-resources nest (`/repos/{id}/tasks`).
Status codes

`201` on create, `204` on delete, **`202 Accepted`** for async work that is
queued but not finished (reindex, reembed, retry), **`409 Conflict`** when a
request can't proceed because the resource is in a conflicting state (e.g. a
repo that is already indexing), `404` for missing resources.
Accepted pragmatic patterns (these are conventional REST, not violations)

**Search / computation with a complex body → `POST .../search`** (and
`/search/paginated`, `code/search`, `code/blast-radius`). A GET query string
can't cleanly or safely carry rich filters or credentials.

**Non-CRUD actions as `POST` sub-resources** — verbs in the path are fine for
actions that are not plain CRUD: `/{id}/merge`, `/{key}/trigger`,
`/{id}/reindex`, `/{name}/test`, `/{id}/retry`, `/reprocess`, `/reason`,
`/completions`, and the auth flows (`/login`, `/logout`, `/refresh`).

**Bulk operations via `POST` with a body** — `POST /memories/batch` (bulk
create) and `POST /memories/delete` (bulk delete). `DELETE`-with-body is poorly
supported by clients/proxies; the bulk-delete reply reports per-id results
(`{deleted, not_found}`) because a missing id is non-fatal. The bulk delete is
also processed server-side **in series** to avoid the graph-cleanup deadlock
that concurrent per-row deletes hit.

**`PUT` on a config singleton/collection** to replace it wholesale
(`/config/llm-providers`, `/llm-profiles`, `/feature-flags`, `/system-prompts`,
`/repos-path`, `/config/theme`) — idempotent full-replace. `GET /config/theme`
is deliberately unauthenticated: the frontend theme loads at boot, before
login, and the payload is pure UI cosmetics.
Naming

**Casing:** lowercase **kebab-case** for every multi-word path segment
(`llm-providers`, `feature-flags`, `pipeline-failures`, `system-prompts`,
`prune-cache`, `retry-all`, `blast-radius`). No snake_case or camelCase appears
in any path. New segments must follow this.

**Pluralization:** collections are plural (`memories`, `repos`, `tags`,
`jobs`, `vectors`, `conversations`, `pipeline-failures`); a sub-resource that
is one-per-parent is singular (`code/graph/{id}`, `code/wiki/{id}`,
`vectors/projection`, `config/*`).

**Nouns for resources, verbs only on action sub-resources** (see the action
pattern above).

Three verb-flavoured names remain (breaking to rename, so left as-is):
`/reembed` (a verb-named maintenance namespace — a noun model would be
`/embeddings` with refresh actions), `/code/symbols/lookup` (a name-based query
better expressed as a filter on `/symbols`), and `/system/fs/list` (reads
imperative; `/fs/entries` would be noun-ish). All are used by the frontend.
GET is safe and idempotent

A `GET` must never change server state. Wiki generation used to run inside
`GET /code/wiki/{repo_id}`; it is now **read-only** (returns the cached wiki or
`null`). Generation is an explicit action: `POST /repos/{repo_id}/reindex` with
`generate_wiki=true`.
Known deviations (intentional, not yet changed — breaking to fix)

These are minor verb/consistency deviations left as-is because changing them
would break existing frontend clients for marginal benefit. Fix only with a
coordinated client update:

`POST /config/llm` sets the six-purpose LLM config (idempotent full replace);
for symmetry with its `PUT` siblings it should be `PUT /config/llm`.

`DELETE /repos/{repo_id}/tasks/{task_id}` cancels a running task; a clearer
model is `POST /repos/{repo_id}/tasks/{task_id}/cancel` (cancel ≠ remove, and
it isn't idempotent in the DELETE sense).

`PUT /repos/{repo_id}` is a partial update; `PATCH` would be more precise and
would harmonize with `PATCH /chat/conversations/{id}`.
2026-06-04 audit fixes

A full-surface RESTful audit (all ~70 endpoints) confirmed the posture above and
landed three fixes: `GET /code/wiki` made read-only (safe GET); `POST
/repos/{id}/reindex` now returns `202` (and `409` when already indexing);
`DELETE /pipeline-failures/{id}` now returns `204`.

darkmem E2E Test Plan

**Execution model:** This plan is a runbook for **Claude Code (me)** to execute via the Playwright MCP tools. Each phase is a user journey with explicit browser steps, expected states, and verification points. Supporting Python scripts in `scripts/` handle API-level checks that are awkward through the browser (bulk ingest, DB audit, performance timing).
**When the user says "run phase N" or "run the full E2E plan":**
Verify Playwright MCP is connected (`browser_navigate` etc. available).
Follow the phase's steps in order, using Playwright tools for UI interaction and Bash for supporting scripts.
Capture a `browser_snapshot` at each verification point and compare against the expected state.
Write observations into the phase's **Execution log** section (in this doc or a sibling file under `docs/e2e/runs/`).
Stop and report any FAIL or unexpected state before moving on — do not batch failures silently.
**Prerequisites:**
Fresh darkmem deployment: backend on `http://localhost:8000`, frontend on `http://host.docker.internal:3636`, admin password NOT set.
Ollama running with the configured embedding model and chat model.
Playwright MCP browser process available via `mcp__playwright__browser_*` tools.
Python 3.12+ with `httpx` in PATH for supporting scripts.
**Fresh state check** (always run first):
`curl http://localhost:8000/api/v1/auth/status` → `{"initialized": false}`
`curl http://localhost:8000/api/v1/analytics/stats` → zeros (or 401, needs auth)
How Claude executes this plan
Standard playwright tools I use

| Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `mcp__playwright__browser_navigate(url)` | Go to a URL |
| `mcp__playwright__browser_snapshot()` | Get accessibility tree of the current page (preferred over screenshots for data extraction) |
| `mcp__playwright__browser_take_screenshot()` | Visual screenshot for design/UX verification |
| `mcp__playwright__browser_click(element, ref)` | Click a button, link, or other element |
| `mcp__playwright__browser_type(element, ref, text)` | Type into an input |
| `mcp__playwright__browser_fill_form(fields)` | Fill multiple form fields at once |
| `mcp__playwright__browser_press_key(key)` | Send Enter, Escape, Tab, etc. |
| `mcp__playwright__browser_wait_for(text)` | Wait for text to appear/disappear |
| `mcp__playwright__browser_console_messages()` | Pull console errors/warnings |
| `mcp__playwright__browser_network_requests()` | Inspect recent HTTP calls |
| `mcp__playwright__browser_resize(w, h)` | Test responsive layouts |
| `mcp__playwright__browser_close()` | **Always** call when finished — shared instance |
Standard flow for each step
Perform the action (navigate / click / type).
Call `browser_snapshot()` and check the expected element/text is present.
If a mutation was triggered, wait for the spinner/toast then re-snapshot.
If an assertion fails, call `browser_console_messages()` and `browser_network_requests()` to capture context before logging the failure.
Move to the next step.
Supporting scripts
For operations that are slow/awkward through the UI (bulk ingest, DB queries, performance timing), run the corresponding script via Bash:

cd docs/e2e/scripts
python 00_health_check.py
python 04_memories_batch_mcp.py --password "e2e-admin-pw"
python 12_perf_baseline.py --password "e2e-admin-pw"
python 13_db_audit.py
Scripts print PASS/FAIL lines I can read from the output. Log their results in the phase's Execution log.

darkmem

A centralized memory system for AI agents: stores and retrieves natural-language
**memories** (semantic + keyword hybrid search over pgvector), builds an
**entity/relationship knowledge graph** from them, and indexes **code
repositories** into a navigable symbol/call graph. It exposes a REST API, a
WebSocket event stream, and an **MCP** tool endpoint for agents, with a React UI.
**Backend:** FastAPI + SQLAlchemy (async) + Postgres/pgvector

**Frontend:** React + TanStack Router/Query (built into the API image and
served by it)

**LLM:** pluggable per-purpose providers (OpenAI-compatible, Ollama, Anthropic,
Google, DeepSeek, z.ai), configured at runtime via the setup wizard
Licensed under Apache-2.0 (see `LICENSE`).
Quickstart (Docker Compose)
Prerequisites: Docker + Docker Compose v2.

cp .env.example .env
# Edit .env and generate the two secrets:
#   DB_PASSWORD   = openssl rand -base64 24
#   JWT_SECRET    = openssl rand -hex 32      (must be >= 32 chars)
# If you reach the UI over plain HTTP on your LAN, also set COOKIE_SECURE=false.
# Pin the image tag for a real deploy:  DARKMEM_VERSION=0.2.0

docker compose up -d

The API boots only after Postgres is healthy, runs database migrations
automatically, then serves everything on `:8000` — the REST API, the WebSocket
stream, the MCP endpoint and the UI itself. There is one container and one port;
nothing binds `:80` or `:3000`. Postgres stays on loopback.

The app is the network edge in this topology: it trusts no proxy headers, and the
login rate limiter keys on the transport peer. The session cookie is `Secure`
(HTTPS-only) by default. To serve over plain HTTP on the LAN, set
`COOKIE_SECURE=false` — note the cookie then travels in cleartext. Putting a
**TLS-terminating reverse proxy** (nginx/Caddy/Traefik) in front is a different
posture, not the default one: that proxy becomes the edge, so set
`TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS=true` as well, or every client will share the proxy's
rate-limit bucket.
First-run setup
Open the UI and complete the setup wizard (`/setup`):
Set the admin password (you authenticate as a single admin).

Configure LLM providers and assign a model to each **purpose** (embedding,
extraction, classification, reasoning, summarization, reranker). LLM config
lives in the database — it is **not** set via environment variables.
Optionally register a repository path to index.

`/setup` is **trust-on-first-use**: it stays open only until the admin password
exists, so the first caller to finish the wizard claims the admin account. Run
setup promptly after first boot on a trusted network.
Configuration reference

All backend settings are environment variables (see `.env.example`). The
production-critical ones:

| Variable | Required in prod | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ENVIRONMENT` | set in compose (`production`) | Arms fail-fast validators (JWT strength) and the default `Secure` cookie. The compose file hardcodes this; you don't set it in `.env`. |
| `DB_PASSWORD` | **yes** | Postgres password. The API derives `DATABASE_URL` from it (host/port/db/user are fixed for the bundled stack). |
| `JWT_SECRET` | **yes** | Session-token signing key. Must be ≥ 32 chars and not a placeholder, or the app refuses to boot. |
| `COOKIE_SECURE` | no (default `true`) | Set `false` to allow login over plain HTTP on a trusted LAN; leave `true` behind HTTPS. |
| `DARKMEM_VERSION` | recommended | Image tag for compose; pin to a release. |
| `LOG_LEVEL` | no | `DEBUG`/`INFO`/`WARNING`/`ERROR` (default `INFO`). |

`DATABASE_URL` is derived from `DB_PASSWORD`; set it explicitly only to point at
an external Postgres. `TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS` defaults to `false` because the app is
the edge; set it to `true` only when a trusted proxy really is in front. Runtime
**LLM configuration is stored in the database** via the setup wizard and the
Settings → LLM Pipeline UI; there are no `LLM_*` env variables.

Both secrets are read at runtime and are baked into no image layer, so rotating
`JWT_SECRET` or `DB_PASSWORD` is "edit `.env`, `docker compose up -d`" — a
container recreate, never an image rebuild.
Operations
Health

`GET /health` is the liveness/readiness probe (used by the compose healthcheck):
`503` when Postgres/pgvector is unreachable, `200` (degraded) when only the LLM
provider is unreachable. The container is `unhealthy` until the API can serve.
Backups (do this before going live)

**All state lives in the `postgres_data` Docker volume.** There is no automatic
backup — losing the volume loses everything. Use the provided scripts and run
them on a schedule (cron):

./scripts/backup.sh /path/to/backups        # writes darkmem-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.sql.gz
./scripts/restore.sh /path/to/backups/darkmem-20260607-030000.sql.gz
Store backups off-host. Always **back up before an upgrade**.
Upgrades
Back up (above).
Pull the new image tag (bump `DARKMEM_VERSION` in `.env`).
`docker compose up -d`.
Migrations run automatically on API startup (`alembic upgrade head`). Notes:

The first upgrade to 0.2.0 runs migration `0003`, which **rebuilds the derived
code graph** (it clears `code_edges`/`code_graph_nodes` and forces a reindex on
next sync). Memories and code symbols are untouched; the graph is regenerated.

Migrations run inline at startup, so run **one API replica at a time** during an
upgrade (the bundled topology is single-replica). Downgrades are not a recovery
path — restore from backup if a migration fails.
Logs & diagnostics

Logs go to the container stdout (`docker compose logs -f darkmem-api`), formatted
with timestamp/level/logger and controlled by `LOG_LEVEL`. Pipeline failures are
recorded in the database and surfaced under Settings → Pipeline. No secrets are
logged (token counts and scrubbed git URLs only).
Security checklist (before exposing beyond loopback)
[ ] `ENVIRONMENT=production` (compose default), strong `JWT_SECRET` (≥32 chars), non-default `DB_PASSWORD`. Run `/setup` promptly — it is open until the admin password is set.

[ ] UI reached only through your TLS reverse proxy (HTTPS); do not publish port 8000 publicly. If you add that proxy, also set `TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS=true` so the rate limiter keys on the client rather than the proxy.
[ ] `/mcp` is the **unauthenticated** agent tool endpoint — keep it on loopback. Never expose it to untrusted networks.
[ ] FastAPI `/docs`, `/redoc`, `/openapi.json` are served unauthenticated — keep them behind the loopback bind / your proxy's auth.
[ ] Provider API keys and git tokens are stored in the database in plaintext (single-operator model) — keep the `postgres_data` volume and backups access-controlled and encrypted at rest.
Development
docker compose -f docker-compose.dev.yml up -d   # builds locally, hot-reload, ports on all interfaces
Backend tests (need a `darkmem_test` database on the dev Postgres):
cd backend && python -m pytest -q
Frontend:
cd frontend && npm ci && npm run typecheck && npx vitest run && npm run build

for design specs and audit reports.
Runbook — break-glass content purge

**Status:** operator procedure, not an application feature. Written 2026-08-06 as rider R2
of T2.59's ruling (option D: accept the residue and document it).
When this applies

Exactly one case: **content that must not exist anywhere** — a pasted credential, a key, a
token, someone else's personal data. Nothing else. Deleting a memory through the API or UI
is the normal path and is sufficient for ordinary removal.
Why this is a procedure and not a button

Darkmem's `events` journal is append-only and enforced as such by three trigger kinds (a
row-level UPDATE/DELETE guard on the parent, a statement-level TRUNCATE guard, and a
per-child TRUNCATE guard stamped by `events_ensure_partition`). That is deliberate: the
journal is the record of what the system did, and a consolidation cycle whose evidence can
be edited afterwards describes a history that did not happen.

Giving the application a code path that rewrites the journal would cost more than the
residue it removes — it would put a "make this never have happened" primitive one bug or
one compromised session away from the audit substrate. **The operator already owns the
database.** This procedure just writes down what that ownership means, so the dangerous
capability lives with the human who has the superuser password rather than in the app.
What the residue actually is

Deleting a memory removes the row, its embeddings (FK cascade), its tags and its graph
contributions. These survive, by design:

| Store | What survives | Bounded? |
|---|---|---|
| `events` payloads | content previews; full refine summaries in `consolidated` / `undone`; contradiction counterpart triples in `verified` | No — append-only |
| `knowledge_triples.fact` | the lifted sentence | No — a fact outlives any one asserting memory |
| `messages.context` | citation snippets, and cited fact rows untrimmed | Until the conversation is deleted |
| `memory_buffer` | raw content on `done` rows | Yes — `buffer_done_retention_hours`, default 24 |

Two remedies already exist and should be tried first: **delete the conversation** (cascades
its snippets and its prose) and **wait out or shorten the buffer retention** (a config row).
The procedure
Read all of it before starting. Steps 1 and 6 are the ones people skip.

**Rotate the secret first.** Everything below is slower than an attacker. Purging the
database does not un-leak a credential that was live; rotating does. If the content is
not a credential, skip to 2.

**Stop the application.** Both the API and any running jobs — a consolidation pass
mid-flight will re-derive from rows you are about to edit.
docker compose down          # or stop the uvicorn process
**Find every occurrence.** Do not guess which stores hold it.

**Edit as superuser with the guards disabled for the session.** `session_replication_role`
suppresses the append-only triggers for this connection only.
**`events` is RANGE-partitioned with a composite `PRIMARY KEY (id, created_at)`.** A bare
`WHERE id = ...` scans every monthly child; always carry the `created_at` bound.
**Reclaim the pages.** An `UPDATE` leaves the old tuple readable on disk until vacuumed.

VACUUM FULL events;      -- takes an exclusive lock; size it against your downtime
VACUUM FULL messages;

**Deal with backups.** This is the step that makes the rest meaningful. Any dump or
volume snapshot taken before the purge still contains the content. Rotate or destroy
them per your retention policy, and record that you did.
**Restart, and verify.** Re-run the step-3 queries and confirm zero rows.
After

Write down what happened and when — ideally as a memory in a project you keep for
operations. A break-glass purge is the one action in this system with no audit trail by
construction, because the audit trail is what it edited.
Runbook — exposing darkmem beyond the LAN

**Who this is for.** An operator putting darkmem behind a TLS proxy so it is
reachable from outside the trusted LAN. Everything here is additive: every LAN
rule below still holds underneath (doc 18 §9).

**darkmem does not terminate TLS and never will.** It has no certificate
handling, no ACME client and no HTTP→HTTPS redirect. The certificate, the
renewal, and the redirect are the operator's proxy's job. If you have not put a
TLS proxy in front, you are not in this posture — stay on the LAN defaults.
1. The one switch, and everything it moves

`TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS=true` is the exposed-deployment switch. It is not only a
rate-limiter setting:

| | LAN default (off) | Exposed (on) |
|---|---|---|
| Login rate-limit bucket | the transport peer | `X-Real-IP`, else the **rightmost** `X-Forwarded-For` hop |
| `cookie_secure` | tri-state: unset ⇒ Secure only when `ENVIRONMENT=production` | **enforced** — an explicit `COOKIE_SECURE=false` is overridden |

The leftmost `X-Forwarded-For` is read in **neither** posture. It is
client-supplied, so a limiter keyed on it would let an attacker rotate the
value per guess and never lock out.

Setting `COOKIE_SECURE=false` alongside `TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS=true` is not an
error and does not stop the app — the value is clamped to `true`, a warning is
logged at startup, and `GET /api/v1/auth/security-posture` reports
`cookie_secure_clamped: true`. If you genuinely serve plain HTTP, leave
`TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS` off; the two settings describe the same fact and must
agree.

**One topology is unsupported, and it is worth saying plainly: a reverse proxy
that does not terminate TLS.** Neither setting is right for it. With the switch
on, the clamped Secure cookie is dropped by the browser over plain HTTP and
login silently loops. With it off, every client shares the proxy's single
limiter bucket, so one attacker locks out everyone. Put TLS on the proxy, or
put nothing in front and let the app be the edge.

**If login loops after you turn the switch on, suspect the clamp first.** Every
report of it except the startup log — the posture endpoint, the settings card —
sits behind the login it just broke, so the boot warning is the one you can
still read. Check the container log for `COOKIE_SECURE=false is clamped`.
2. What your proxy must do
**Terminate TLS**, and redirect plain HTTP to it.

**Set `X-Real-IP` to its own view of the peer**, overwriting whatever the
client sent. If the client can supply this header through your proxy, the
lockout is defeated and turning the switch on has made things worse than
leaving it off.

**Append to `X-Forwarded-For`, never replace it** — the app reads the
rightmost hop, which must be the one your proxy added.

**Send the credential as `Authorization: Bearer`.** The webhook authenticates
the *caller*, not a signature over the payload — which it never parses, since
the pipeline re-derives the true state with its own `git pull` and HEAD
compare. The consequence to plan around: **GitHub.com's native webhook
delivery cannot set an `Authorization` header**, so it cannot reach this
receiver. Self-hosted senders that can — Gitea, a `post-receive` script,
a small relay — can.

**Do not route `/mcp` from the public side** — and the app now refuses it
rather than trusting you not to. `/mcp` is unauthenticated by design
(local-network trust model); its only network defence is the DNS-rebinding
Host allowlist, and the bearer-required option for that door is designed but
**not shipped** (doc 18 §5). Publishing `/mcp` would publish every MCP tool
to anyone who can reach it. So with `TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS=true`, a `/mcp`
request carrying proxy headers is answered `403 mcp_not_exposed` and
journalled as `mcp_proxied_refused` (throttled to one row a minute, so a
scanner cannot grow the journal). Restrict it at the proxy as well; this
guard is the backstop, not the plan.
**Extending `MCP_ALLOWED_HOSTS` does not lift it.** That is deliberate. The
standing advice for a LAN `421` is to extend the allowlist, and without this
guard that advice — correct for its own problem — was one entry away from
publishing `/mcp`. A LAN or local agent reaching the box directly is
untouched in both postures.
3. Credentials for programmatic callers

Non-human callers use an API key — `Authorization: Bearer dmk_<key_id>_<secret>`
— minted from the settings UI, with a closed scope set (`capture`, `read`,
`admin`). The plaintext is shown once at issue. `ratify` is not a scope and
never becomes one: confirming a fact stays a human cookie session on the REST
door.

**What each scope reaches, exactly.** The scope-gated surface is small on
purpose, and it is the surface the minimal client speaks:

| Scope | Routes |
|---|---|
| `capture` | `POST /memories`, `POST /memories/batch` |
| `read` | `POST /memories/search/paginated` |
| `admin` | `POST /repos/{id}/webhook` |

Everything else stays human-session-only. That is a deliberate boundary rather
than an oversight: widening `read` to the fact vault or the code graph decides
what a leaked key can exfiltrate, so it happens when something needs it. Grant
the narrowest scope that does the job — a webhook sender needs `admin` and
nothing else.

Revoke a key from the same surface. Revocation sets `revoked_at` and keeps the
row rather than deleting it, so calls the key already made keep a resolvable
name instead of pointing at an id nothing explains.

**Detecting a key you did not expect to be in use.** Every keyed delivery
journals a `repo_webhook_received` event carrying the key id and its label —
including deliveries that are refused as conflicts or that name a repository
that does not exist, which is what a probing credential mostly produces. The
settings card's last-used column is the quick signal; the events journal is the
record. A key whose last-used time moves when you are not deploying is the
signal to revoke.

Note the scope of that: the webhook is currently the **only** route a key
reaches, so key activity appears in the events journal and not on a memory's
own timeline — no keyed call can write a memory today.
4. Verify the posture you think you have
With an authenticated session, read the live posture rather than assuming it:
GET /api/v1/auth/security-posture
Expect, in this posture:
`trust_proxy_headers: true`

`cookie_secure: true` (and `cookie_secure_clamped: true` if you also set
`COOKIE_SECURE=false`)
`mcp_allowed_hosts` listing exactly the hosts you intend

Then confirm the limiter is really keyed on the proxied address: make
`rate_limit_max_failures` failed logins from one client, confirm the next
attempt returns `429`, and confirm a request from a different source address
still returns `401`. If the `429` never arrives, your proxy is not setting
`X-Real-IP` the way §2 requires.
5. What does not change

The MCP Host allowlist (a foreign Host is `421`, fixed by extending the
allowlist — never by setting `*`), trust-on-first-use setup then `403`,
single-door ratification, and the single-worker invariant. Exposure layers on
top of these; it replaces none of them.
